/-!
# Can a prime $p$ satisfy $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ and $3^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$?

A prime $p$ with $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is a Wieferich prime (the only known examples
are $1093$ and $3511$). A prime $p$ with $3^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is a Mirimanoff prime
(the only known examples are $11$ and $1006003$). It is an open question whether a prime can
satisfy both congruences simultaneously. Lenstra gave a heuristic argument against this.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [Wikipedia, Wieferich prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wieferich_prime)
* J. B. Dobson, [On Lerch's formula for the Fermat quotient](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.3907v6)
* [OEIS A001220](https://oeis.org/A001220) (Wieferich primes)
* [OEIS A014127](https://oeis.org/A014127) (Mirimanoff primes)
-/

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no existence question (does a prime exist that is simultaneously a base-2 Wieferich prime and a base-3 Wieferich/Mirimanoff prime, i.e. p^2 | 2^(p-1)-1 and p^2 | 3^(p-1)-1); the Prop is `∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 2^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2] ∧ 3^(p-1) ≡ 1 [MOD p^2]` stated with `answer(sorry) ↔ ...` since the answer is unknown (only Lenstra's heuristic argues against existence); no extra hypothesis excluding p = 2, 3 is needed since the congruences fail for them automatically, and no small-p or ZMod 0 boundary issues arise because p is prime.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the slot identically (modulo cosmetic `(2 : ℕ)` ascriptions and line breaks): `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ 2 ^ (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 2] ∧ 3 ^ (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 2]`. This is a faithful rendering of the verbatim yes/no question: answer(True) = such a prime exists, answer(False) = none does; the existential uses ∧ (not →) so the answer is genuinely constrained. Boundary cases: `p.Prime` forces p ≥ 2 so `p - 1` does not truncate and the modulus `p ^ 2 ≥ 4` is finite (no ZMod 0 issue); `Nat.ModEq` on ℕ coincides with the integer congruence since all terms are nonnegative; p = 2, 3 fail the congruences automatically so no extra exclusion is needed. c04 chosen because it adds accurate, source-backed context (Wieferich 1093/3511, Mirimanoff 11/1006003, Lehmer 1938, Lenstra heuristic — all confirmed in the cited arXiv paper 1103.3907) plus `test`-category sanity theorems (1093 satisfies base-2; 11 satisfies base-3 but not base-2; 2 and 3 satisfy neither) that guard the encoding. Uses Copyright 2026 (current year); compiles with only the `sorry` warning.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Can a prime $p$ satisfy $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ and $3^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$?

A prime $p$ with $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is a Wieferich prime (the only known examples
are $1093$ and $3511$). A prime $p$ with $3^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is a Mirimanoff prime
(the only known examples are $11$ and $1006003$). It is an open question whether a prime can
satisfy both congruences simultaneously. Lenstra gave a heuristic argument against this.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [Wikipedia, Wieferich prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wieferich_prime)
* J. B. Dobson, [On Lerch's formula for the Fermat quotient](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.3907v6)
* [OEIS A001220](https://oeis.org/A001220) (Wieferich primes)
* [OEIS A014127](https://oeis.org/A014127) (Mirimanoff primes)
-/

namespace CanAPrimePSatisfy2P1Equiv1PmodP2And3P1Equiv1PmodP2

/--
Can a prime $p$ satisfy $2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ and $3^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$
simultaneously? That is, does there exist a prime $p$ that is both a Wieferich prime and a
Mirimanoff prime?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem can_a_prime_p_satisfy_2_p_1_equiv_1_pmod_p_2_and_3_p_1_equiv_1_pmod_p_2 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ 2 ^ (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 2] ∧ 3 ^ (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 2] := by
  sorry

/-- The prime $1093$ is a Wieferich prime: $2^{1092} \equiv 1 \pmod{1093^2}$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem two_pow_modEq_one_1093 : 2 ^ (1093 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 1093 ^ 2] := by
  decide +kernel

/-- The prime $11$ is a Mirimanoff prime: $3^{10} \equiv 1 \pmod{11^2}$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem three_pow_modEq_one_11 : 3 ^ (11 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 11 ^ 2] := by
  decide

/-- The prime $11$ is not a Wieferich prime: $2^{10} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{11^2}$. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_two_pow_modEq_one_11 : ¬ 2 ^ (11 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 11 ^ 2] := by
  decide

/-- The primes $2$ and $3$ satisfy neither congruence, so no hypothesis excluding them is needed
in the statement of the problem. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_modEq_two_three :
    ¬ 2 ^ (2 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 2 ^ 2] ∧ ¬ 3 ^ (2 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 2 ^ 2] ∧
      ¬ 2 ^ (3 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 3 ^ 2] ∧ ¬ 3 ^ (3 - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD 3 ^ 2] := by
  decide

end CanAPrimePSatisfy2P1Equiv1PmodP2And3P1Equiv1PmodP2

items: The yes/no question is encoded as `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ p, ...` following the repository's convention for questions stated in English; `answer(True)` corresponds to a positive answer (a prime satisfying both congruences exists).

Congruences are expressed with `Nat.ModEq` (`a ≡ b [MOD n]`) over ℕ with modulus `p ^ 2`; since `p.Prime` forces `p ≥ 2`, the natural-number subtraction `p - 1` does not truncate and the modulus is never 0.

No hypothesis excluding p = 2 or p = 3 is added, since both congruences fail for those primes automatically (verified by a `test`-category theorem in the file), matching the decomposition table's note.

Added `test`-category theorems: 1093 satisfies the base-2 congruence (proved by `decide +kernel` because the exponent 1092 exceeds the default `decide`/`norm_num` exponent threshold), 11 satisfies the base-3 congruence but not the base-2 one, and p = 2, 3 satisfy neither.
The arXiv reference https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.3907v6 is attributed to J. B. Dobson, as given in the paper's LaTeX source.
